claims.text: The premelting and melting behavior of Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by their degree of atomic-scale chemical ordering.
A homogeneous, random elemental distribution gives these nanoparticles higher cohesive energy than an elementally segregated distribution.
Nanoparticles retaining a homogeneous elemental distribution have a delayed premelting onset.
Nanoparticles retaining a homogeneous elemental distribution have a sharper melting transition.
Elemental segregation causes an earlier onset of premelting.
Elemental segregation broadens the melting regime.
The initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are synthesized as a homogeneous random solid solution.
Thermal pretreatment can induce controlled variations in elemental segregation within the nanoparticles.
The spatial distribution of the constituent elements mediates the cohesive-energy landscape of the nanoparticles.
A homogeneous elemental distribution maximizes cohesive bonding through higher configurational entropy.
The proposed increase in cohesive bonding raises the energy required to initiate atomic mobility.
Elemental segregation creates regions with locally weakened bonding.
Locally weakened bonding reduces the energy barrier for premelting.
Locally weakened bonding broadens the melting transition.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to particles smaller than 100 nm under inert atmospheres and controlled heating rates.
Particle size, ambient atmosphere, and compositional extremes may alter the proposed behavior.

Failure of confirmed segregated particles to show both a statistically significant reduction in premelting onset and a broadened transition relative to the homogeneous control would falsify the hypothesis.
